Early development in Pink salmon begins with the incubation of eggs within gravel redds at cool water temperatures. Embryos develop at an average temperature of 9 °C [T = 9 °C], with the alevins emerging from the gravel after approximately 60 days [ab = approximately 60 days]. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva, or alevin, continues to absorb its yolk reserves while remaining in the interstitial spaces of the streambed. Upon yolk-sac resorption, the exotrophic transition occurs when the fry emerge and begin active feeding. During this initial stage, the wet weight at birth is recorded at approximately 0.1575 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.1575 grams], reflecting the modest energy reserves packaged into the egg. This value is comparable to that observed in congeneric species such as Oncorhynchus keta, from which the estimate is partially derived. Following emergence, the young fry must rapidly locate suitable rearing habitat to begin exogenous feeding on aquatic invertebrates, a critical period marked by high mortality.

As Pink salmon progress through their first year of life, they undergo rapid growth in freshwater before migrating to the marine environment. The parr stage is characterized by increasing body size and the development of smoltification, which prepares the fish for the physiological demands of saltwater. During this juvenile phase, individuals experience an accelerated growth phase driven by abundant prey resources in the ocean. The species does not spend an extended period in freshwater after emergence, instead migrating downstream relatively quickly compared to other Pacific salmon. Once in the marine environment, feeding intensity increases dramatically, supporting the accumulation of somatic tissue. This period of rapid mass gain continues until the fish approach the size at which they will become reproductively mature. Field surveys indicate that by the time individuals reach sexual maturity, their body length has increased considerably from the few centimeters observed at emergence.

The reproductive biology of Pink salmon is defined by a strict semelparous life history, wherein individuals spawn once and then die. Sexual maturation occurs after a relatively brief oceanic residence, typically spanning two years. At the onset of puberty, females attain a total length of approximately 45 centimeters [Lp = approximately 45 centimeters], a size that reflects the energetic investment in gonadal development. Concomitantly, the wet weight at puberty averages around 1,420 grams [Wwp = around 1,420 grams], derived from allometric relationships observed in field-caught specimens. The gonadal mass of maturing females increases substantially as vitellogenesis proceeds, producing a large complement of eggs. As spawning approaches, the fish cease feeding altogether and undergo dramatic morphological changes, including the development of a pronounced hump and an elongated, hooked jaw known as a kype. These secondary sexual characteristics are most pronounced in males and are linked to competition for access to spawning females.

Spawning takes place in shallow gravel riffles of coastal streams, where females excavate nests called redds using powerful sweeps of their tail. A single female deposits all of her eggs within a single redd, after which the male fertilizes them externally. At the end of life, a female produces approximately 2,000 eggs  when spawning occurs at a water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This fecundity value is typical for the species and is lower than that of larger-bodied Pacific salmon such as Chinook salmon, reflecting the constrained body size of Pink salmon. After spawning, both sexes quickly deteriorate and die from physiological exhaustion, completing their life cycle. The eggs incubate through the winter, with the timing of hatching closely tied to the prevailing thermal regime of the stream. The entire reproductive effort is thus compressed into a single, high-investment event, with no possibility of future breeding.

The maximum size attained by Pink salmon reflects the constraints of their short, two-year life cycle under the thermal conditions typical of their range. The ultimate total length observed in wild populations reaches approximately 76 centimeters [Li = approximately 76 centimeters], a value that represents the upper limit of somatic growth before terminal maturation. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight reaches about 7,130 grams [Wwi = about 7,130 grams], though this estimate carries some uncertainty due to variation in oceanic feeding conditions among different stocks. The lifespan of these fish in the wild is fixed at approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years], a duration that includes the freshwater incubation, rearing, and the oceanic feeding phase before the return migration at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This compressed life history, enacted at typical North Pacific temperatures of around 7 °C [T = 7 °C], is among the shortest of any Pacific salmon species and underpins their population dynamics and fishery management strategies.

Pink salmon exhibit a distinctive population structure that is tightly coupled to their strict two-year life cycle, creating a pattern of alternating year classes known as odd-year and even-year runs. These two genetically distinct lineages display subtle differences in body size, fecundity, and timing of spawning migration, reflecting adaptation to local stream conditions. The ecological role of Pink salmon extends beyond their individual life history, as their annual spawning migrations deliver a massive pulse of marine-derived nutrients to freshwater and riparian ecosystems, influencing the productivity of entire watersheds across their North Pacific range.
